Day 63 of 100 · Docker

Docker Images

#100DaysOfCloudAndSecurityDockerPublished journey entry

Docker images are content-addressed, layered filesystem artifacts used as immutable bases for containers; tags are movable labels while digests identify exact image content.

Architecture / mental model

Dockerfile / pull → image layers → tag or digest → container writable layer

How it works

Image layers allow filesystem content to be reused between images and builds. A later layer does not rewrite an earlier layer; it describes another filesystem change layered on top.

Tags such as `1.0` or `latest` are human-friendly references and can be moved to new image content. A digest identifies a particular manifest/content address and is therefore stronger when reproducibility requires exact identity.

Build cache effectiveness depends on instruction order. Expensive stable dependency steps should generally occur before frequently changing application source when that ordering is correct for the build.

Hands-on reference

docker image ls
docker image inspect nginx:alpine
docker history nginx:alpine
docker pull nginx:alpine

Verification

Inspect the image ID/digest before and after a pull or rebuild and compare `docker history` output. Prove that a tag can refer to different content over time while an immutable digest identifies one version.

Field note / gotcha

`latest` is just a tag. It is not proof that an image is newest, patched or even related to the most recent release.

Security considerations

Prefer trusted registries and pinned digests for sensitive/reproducible deployments, scan images, remove unnecessary packages and avoid baking credentials into layers because deleting them in a later layer does not remove them from earlier image history.

What I learned

Reproducibility depends on image identity, not the comforting English meaning of a tag name.
